pr_title: feat(autoware_behavior_velocity_traffic_light_module): support arrow-aware passing judgment on yellow signal
pr_contents: This PR improves the stop/pass judgment logic for yellow signals in turn lanes equipped with traffic light arrows. It prevents unnecessary stops when the signal transitions from "Green" to "Yellow," enabling smoother traffic flow.

Currently, when a traffic light transitions in the sequence of "Green -> Yellow -> Red + Arrow" while the vehicle is in a left/right turn lane, the system generates a stop line during the Yellow phase, causing the vehicle to stop. This behavior can obstruct traffic flow in situations where the vehicle should ideally proceed through the intersection on yellow to complete the turn (or wait for the arrow signal inside the intersection).
Introduced a logic to allow passing on a yellow signal under specific conditions by combining static map information with dynamic signal state transitions.

pr_contents: The naming of the `enable_obstruction_prevention` parameter was misleading. While it suggested control over all obstruction prevention, its effect was limited to intersections. Specifically, setting enable_obstruction_prevention to false would only skip the main obstruction prevention logic at intersections with traffic lights.
This led to an issue where, if a location was not classified as an intersection, the obstruction prevention logic would not be skipped, regardless of the parameter's setting.

To address this, the `enable_obstruction_prevention` parameter has been repurposed to globally disable the entire feature. A new parameter, `ignore_in_intersection`, has been introduced to replicate the previous behavior of skipping the logic specifically at intersections.

A bag file was run on a non-intersection crosswalk, confirming that when the parameter is set to false, the crosswalk module's obstruction prevention feature does not activate, even in the presence of a stopped vehicle.

pr_title: feat(autoware_lidar_frnet): integrate cuda blackboard into point clooud process
pr_contents: This PR integrates CUDA blackboard into the `autoware_lidar_frnet` package to optimize point cloud processing performance by eliminating unnecessary CPU↔GPU memory transfers.

This implementation eliminates CPU↔GPU memory transfers throughout the point cloud processing pipeline when both publisher and subscriber support CUDA blackboard, significantly reducing latency and CPU load. When CUDA blackboard is not supported by connected nodes, the system automatically falls back to standard ROS 2 communication for backward compatibility.

pr_details: **CUDA Blackboard Integration**: Replaced standard ROS 2 publishers/subscribers with `CudaBlackboardSubscriber` and `CudaBlackboardPublisher` for direct GPU memory communication
**Input data**: Changed from `cudaMemcpyAsync(..., cudaMemcpyHostToDevice)` (CPU→GPU) to direct GPU memory access via CUDA blackboard
**Output data**: Changed from `cudaMemcpyAsync(..., cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost)` (GPU→CPU) to `cudaMemcpyAsync(..., cudaMemcpyDeviceToDevice)` (GPU→GPU) transfers
Ran the entire sensing module with `/sensing/lidar/concatenated/pointcloud` as input, operating in the same container
Played back actual rosbag data and verified that the "negotiation message has been received" log message was successfully obtained as follows:
Ran the entire sensing module with `/sensing/lidar/concatenated/pointcloud` as input, operating in the same container

Played back actual rosbag data and used terminal commands (e.g., `ros2 topic echo`) to check the output topic `/sensing/lidar/filtered`, verifying that point cloud data was being published correctly without errors. This confirms that the fallback to standard ROS 2 communication (via CPU memory) works correctly when the subscriber (terminal command) doesn't support CUDA blackboard

The input topic is subscribed via CUDA blackboard. If upstream nodes also support CUDA blackboard, GPU memory will be shared directly. Otherwise, standard ROS 2 communication (via CPU memory) will be used automatically through negotiation

**Important**: For CUDA blackboard to work, the subscriber node must be in the same container as the publisher node. This is a prerequisite as it relies on shared GPU memory within the same process/container

The output topics are also published via CUDA blackboard. Downstream nodes that support CUDA blackboard can receive data directly on GPU memory, while nodes that don't support it will receive data via standard ROS 2 communication (CPU memory)
If the input point cloud size is large, you need to modify ml_package_frnet.param.yaml and regenerate the engine
**User-facing topic names remain unchanged**: The original topic names (`~/input/pointcloud`, `~/output/pointcloud/*`) are preserved for backward compatibility

**Automatic negotiation**: CUDA blackboard automatically negotiates with connected nodes. If both publisher and subscriber support CUDA blackboard, GPU memory is shared directly. Otherwise, standard ROS 2 communication (via CPU memory) is used
**Backward compatibility**: Existing nodes that don't support CUDA blackboard will continue to work without modification
**Performance improvement**: Reduced CPU↔GPU memory transfers, improving processing latency (when both publisher and subscriber support CUDA blackboard)
**CPU load reduction**: Eliminated need for copying to host memory, reducing CPU load (when both publisher and subscriber support CUDA blackboard)

**Backward compatibility**: If upstream or downstream nodes don't support CUDA blackboard, standard ROS 2 communication (via CPU memory) will be used automatically through negotiation. This ensures compatibility with existing nodes

pr_title: feat(predicted_path_postprocessor): add a processor to refine penetration by static objects
pr_contents: This pull request introduces a new processor, `RefinePenetrationByStaticObjects`, to the predicted path postprocessor package. This processor refines predicted paths by considering penetration into static objects, improving path prediction accuracy in the presence of static obstacles. The changes include implementation, configuration, schema updates, and documentation for the new processor, as well as some codebase refactoring to support interpolation function reuse.

pr_details: **`autoware_generic_value_calibrator`**: Generic calibration node that learns the mapping between arbitrary float64 input values and vehicle acceleration using Recursive Least Squares (RLS) algorithm.

**`autoware_generic_value_converter`**: Generic conversion node that converts acceleration commands to arbitrary float64 output values using bilinear interpolation on a calibrated velocity-acceleration mapping table.
**Generic Input/Output**: Works with `tier4_debug_msgs::msg::Float64Stamped` instead of vehicle-specific messages
**Topic Converter**: Python utility to convert common message types (Control, Odometry, etc.) to Float64Stamped
**Generic Float64Stamped Interface**: Chose `Float64Stamped` over vehicle-specific messages to maximize flexibility for custom actuators.
**Topic Converter**: Python script for easy integration without code changes, supporting common Autoware message types.
**Default Map Generation**: Simple linear relationship (`accel = value`) as starting point, updated by RLS during calibration.
**Custom Actuator Support**: Enables calibration and control of non-standard actuators (electric motors, hydraulic systems, etc.) without modifying core Autoware code.
**Flexible Calibration**: Supports arbitrary input value ranges, not limited to traditional throttle/brake pedal values.
**Easy Integration**: Topic converter allows using existing Autoware messages (Control, Odometry) without code changes.

pr_contents: This PR fixes the handling of Z-coordinate data in the diffusion planner by properly preserving Z-coordinates throughout the pipeline while maintaining compatibility with the neural network that expects 33-dimensional input without Z-coordinates.
The trajectory and markers are output at a height slightly above the lanelet. They are also significantly affected by roll and pitch.
The trajectory and markers are output at the same height as the lanelet. They are hardly affected by roll or pitch.
This change may cause strange behavior in environments with overpasses.

pr_title: feat: visualization related packages support jazzy
pr_contents: This PR fixes compilation errors in two visualization packages:
The package was using manual `qt5_wrap_cpp()` to handle Qt MOC processing, which generated incorrect file paths and caused build failures:
The `detected_objects_wf_display.hpp` header file contains the `Q_OBJECT` macro (line 51), which requires MOC processing to enable Qt's meta-object system (signals/slots, properties, reflection).
The code was directly calling `Camera::setOrientation()`, which is deprecated in newer versions of Ogre:
This caused compilation to fail because warnings are treated as errors (`-Werror=deprecated-declarations`).
Replaced manual `qt5_wrap_cpp()` with CMake's automatic MOC processing:
Changed from directly setting orientation on the Camera to using the Camera's parent SceneNode:

pr_contents: :warning: THIS PR MUST BE MERGED `autoware_launch` SIDE TOGETHER :warning:

This PR introduces a heartbeat monitoring enhancement to support both manual and remote control modes, ensuring compatibility with ADAPI version 1.9.0 and above. The enhancement corrects previous issues with the `TimeoutDiag` constructor and the `diagnostic_updater` method `add`. These corrections allow for accurate monitoring of the heartbeat signal during remote control, including ADAPI operations.
Doing tests by using remote control. Will be updated as the tests are done.
Review the integration of heartbeat diagnostics, especially focusing on the handling of `TimeoutDiag` and the interaction with the `diagnostic_updater`.

The system now includes robust heartbeat monitoring for both manual and remote control modes. It ensures better reliability when operating with the newer ADAPI versions, reducing the risk of missed heartbeat signals during operation.

pr_title: fix(external_velocity_limit_selector): correctly handle clear command on empty table
pr_contents: This PR fixes a logical bug in the ExternalVelocityLimitSelectorNode.

When a VelocityLimitClearCommand is received while the internal velocity_limit_table_ is empty, the node fails to update its internal state (hardest_limit_). This causes a stale or uninitialized velocity limit to be published, which can lead to incorrect behavior (e.g., the speed limit dropping to 0 km/h in RViz).

The fix ensures that updateVelocityLimit() is always called after a clear command, even if the table is empty. This guarantees that the node's state is reset to a valid default and the correct limit is published.

pr_contents: A new collision checker, referred to as Spheric Collision Detector (SCD) is proposed. The method approximates the ego-vehicle and its surrounding objects using a set of spheres, thereby simplifying collision detection to a mere distance evaluation.

The proposed algorithm is similar to OCC; However unlike OCC it does not rely on point cloud data for object representation. Instead it uses the length and width of objects to construct the spherical approximation. This approach has proven effective for detecting collisions, particularly in emergency situations.
Experimental results were simulated using CARLA(0.9.15), Autoware(2024.01) and ROS 2 bridges. They indicate that the proposed approach is at least 200 times faster than OCC.
To top all this, the algorithm was also tested in PixKit 2.0, an autonomous driving and development vehicle using a 5-foot inflated jumbo beach ball.

We start by computing the braking distance, $s_b$, which is the distance the vehicle travels after the brakes are applied. It is defined as $|v|^2/2.0 * a$ - deduced from the equation of motion, where $v$ is the initial velocity of the ego-vehicle and $a$, the maximum deceleration required for the ego to stop. The thinking distance, $s_t$, is the distance the ego travels in the time it takes for the brakes to be applied after realizing that there is a need to stop. It is defined as $v * t_d$,  with $t_d$ as the delay time. The stopping distance is the sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance.
Next, we select consecutive trajectory points spaced at one sphere diameter apart. This reduces computation cost as collision checks are performed only on these sampled points.
In this step only the segment of the resampled trajectory within the stopping distance is considered.
For each of the trajectory points, their respective footprints are computed using the below expressions:
Subsequently, we generate spheres, and place them on the ego's footprints.

We also approximate the objects surrounding the ego-vehicle using spheres. Each object's footprint is derived from its length and width. Uniform spheres are then generated and placed along an object's center-line, with their relative centers defined as follows:
We set the radius of each sphere to half the vehicle's width.

pr_details: We loop through each distinct sphere pair, $(s_{i}, s_{j})$ of the ego-vehicle and the obstacle, where $1 \leq i \leq m$, $1 \leq j \leq n$. $m$ and $n$ denote the number of spheres of the obstacle and the ego-vehicle respectively.
At each iteration, the Euclidean distance, $\varepsilon_{ij}$, between the centers of the spheres, $c_i(x,y,z)$ and $c_j(x,y,z)$, is calculated.

We then compare $\varepsilon_{ij}$ with the sum of the radii of the respective spheres, $ \sum r_i r_j$. If this distance is less, the diagnostic status is set to ERROR as a collision is imminent; otherwise, we repeat \textit{step 2} for the next pair of spheres. The diagnostic status is set to OK if no collision is detected.

pr_details: The Waypoint Maker is designed to support the Waypoint Following scenario, alongside lane driving and parking. Its architecture consists of two roles: Waypoint Saver, which records odometry into waypoints with a fixed distance interval and stores them in CSV files, and Waypoint Loader, which loads and parses CSV files to generate a path for following. The loader supports both forward and reverse path selection using the same waypoints and integrates with downstream modules such as the Path Smoother, Path Optimizer, and a dedicated Motion Velocity Planner. The scenario is activated when the vehicle is inside or near a defined waypoint zone, and the Scenario Selector manages the transition between waypoint following and other scenarios.

To integrate with the overall planning stack, the Scenario Gate introduces a plugin mechanism for selecting Scenario Selectors and Scenario Planners through configuration. The default selector remains available for lane driving and parking to ensure backward compatibility, while new scenarios such as Waypoint Following can be added as plugins without modifying the original architecture.
Subscribes to vehicle odometry, records waypoints with a configurable distance interval, and stores them in CSV files. The latest recording is also saved as waypoint_default.csv for convenience.

In addition to its backend functionality, the Waypoint Saver provides a simple GUI interface with SAVE and FINISH buttons to make waypoint recording more intuitive. Users can configure the recording distance interval (default: 0.5 meters). Once the SAVE button is clicked, the system begins recording waypoints and displays the current file name being generated. The FINISH button then becomes available, allowing users to stop recording and finalize the waypoint file. For convenience, the most recently recorded waypoint file is also copied as waypoint_default.csv, ensuring the Waypoint Loader can directly access the latest recording without additional manual steps.

Loads and parses CSV files to generate a path for following. It supports both forward and reverse path generation using the same waypoints and integrates with downstream modules such as the Path Smoother, Path Optimizer, and a dedicated Motion Velocity Planner. The loader monitors the ego vehicle’s progress and determines scenario completion once the end waypoint is reached.

In addition to its backend functionality, the Waypoint Loader also provides a GUI interface for user interaction. Through the GUI, users can browse and select waypoint files from a designated folder. Once a file is chosen, clicking the LOAD button will load the waypoints and update waypoint_default.csv to the selected file, ensuring it will be used as the default in future sessions without requiring manual reloading. For safety, the LOAD button is automatically disabled when the vehicle is in motion, preventing accidental file switching during driving.
This design ensures backward compatibility while enabling extensibility for project-specific scenarios such as waypoint following.

The mission_planner dispatches trajectories from LaneDriving (behavior_path_planner, behavior_velocity_planner, motion_velocity_planner), Parking (freespace_planner), and optional extra scenarios. All these trajectories are sent to scenario_gate.
The original scenario selection logic is preserved by wrapping it as a default selector plugin, so the system behaves exactly the same as before.
scenario_gate can load the selector as a plugin. By default, it uses the default selector, but other selectors or planners can also be configured via YAML without modifying existing code or topics.
The final selected trajectory is published to /planning/scenario_planning/trajectory together with /planning/current_scenario, and then processed by the velocity_smoother.
Goal Setup: The user sets a goal pose directly. The system generates a path that brings the vehicle to a stop alongside the designated waypoint zone.
Activation: When the vehicle is detected to be alongside or within the waypoint zone, the scenario automatically switches to Waypoint Following.
Waypoint Execution: The vehicle follows the pre-recorded waypoints. This allows it to traverse through the defined zone using the path generated by the Waypoint Saver/Loader.
Completion & Transition: Once the end of the waypoint path is reached, the system automatically switches back to Lane Driving or Parking depending on the context.

pr_title: feat(autoware_freespace_planner): enhance freespace planner search algorithm and add reparking feature for improved parking accuracy
pr_contents: Refine the A* algorithm’s heuristic function so that the generated trajectory becomes progressively straighter as it approaches the final goal, reducing the controller’s tracking burden and thereby minimizing the final pose error.

The yaw weight (yaw_weight), the distance to the goal extension line (distance_to_goal_extension_weight), and the curvature of the planned path (extra_steering_penalty_factor) will all have increasing penalty weights as the planning distance gets closer to the goal.
This approach produces a straighter path near the goal, enabling the vehicle controller to approach the goal in as straight a manner as possible during actual driving.
The distance difference between the vehicle and the goal’s extension line, used to help the vehicle align with the goal earlier and reverse in a straight line.

In addition to the distance from the goal’s extension line, the goal’s orientation angle should also be aligned in advance to reduce the yaw difference (yaw_diff) and ensure minimal skew when parking.

Emulate human behavior by adding a reparking feature: if the vehicle’s final parking orientation exceeds a specified deviation threshold, trigger a secondary parking maneuver that generates a combined pull‑out-and‑alignment trajectory to correct the angle. Allow up to three corrective attempts to iteratively reduce the error, while alleviating path constraints imposed by nearby obstacles.

The Arrival Checker determines whether the vehicle has reached its destination. However, it does not take into account that in the Parking state, the completion of the parking process must first be verified by the Freespace Planner. As a result, when the vehicle is close enough to the destination and stationary, it may be forcibly switched to a stopped state due to this check.
A new condition has now been added: if the current state is in the Parking procedure, the system must wait for the parking_completed message.​
Once the vehicle has stopped at the goal, if the degree of misalignment exceeds the acceptable threshold (parking_accuracy_tolerance), the reparking function will be activated.

It will replan a straight path moving outward, increasing the weights for alignment (reparking_alignment_weight) and deviation (reparking_deviation_penalty) to slightly correct the angle, align the vehicle, and then approach the goal again.
This process will run for a maximum of three cycles, and if any cycle results in a misalignment smaller than parking_accuracy_tolerance, the parking procedure will be considered complete.
This PR has been tested in Psim.

pr_title: feat(autoware_motion_velocity_obstacle_cruise_module): add obstacle cruise filter time-varying range
pr_contents: So far, the obstacle_cruise_module evaluates every obstacle within the lateral range in front of the ego car's trajectory. However, the maximum sensing range is approximately 120 meters. The detection of obstacles is very noisy at that distance, which can lead to incorrect behavior sometimes. And sometimes the RSS distance is only several dozen meters, much shorter than 120m. Therefore, it's not necessary to evaluate obstacles that are so far away, such as those above 100m.
So, a varying obstacle filter range is introduced here to filter the unnecessary obstacles based on ego_vel, ego_acc, ego_jerk and obstacle_vel.
I used this table to pick out a min/max value (65m/120m) for safe filter range, and varying inside this range. The max_jerk is chosen as 0.15 according to the table.

When the obstacle_cruise virtual wall first appeared, we can tell the difference of the obstacle filter range according to different obstacle_vel. This confirms the obstacle filter range is time-varying now.

pr_title: fix(behavior_path_planner): prevent segfault in updateBoundary with index validation
pr_contents: This PR addresses a critical segmentation fault that occurs in the `behavior_path_planner`, specifically within the static obstacle avoidance module. The crash happens during the process of modifying the drivable area boundary when multiple static obstacles are present, causing the `component_container_mt` process to die.
The crash is identified by the following stack trace, which points to an issue within the `updateBoundary` function.
The root cause of the segmentation fault lies in the `updateBoundary` function located in `drivable_area_expansion/static_drivable_area.cpp`.
This function modifies the drivable area's boundary (`updated_bound`) by iterating through a list of obstacle polygons and removing sections of the boundary vector using `std::vector::erase()`.
The core of the problem is as follows:
To resolve this issue, this PR introduces a guard clause to validate the indices right before calling `updated_bound.erase()`.

This check ensures that both the start and end indices for the erase operation are within the valid range of the `updated_bound` vector's current size. If the indices are invalid, the operation for that particular polygon is skipped, and an error is logged. This prevents the crash while maintaining the integrity of the drivable area generation process.

[component_container_mt-94] *** SIGABRT (@0x3e800001dd0) received by PID 7632 (TID 0x7f81e0ff1640) from PID 7632; stack trace: ***

[ERROR] [component_container_mt-94]: process has died [pid 7632, exit code -6, cmd '/home/autoware/autoware.proj/install/rclcpp_components/lib/rclcpp_components/component_container_mt --ros-args -r __node:=behavior_planning_container -r __ns:=/planning/scenario_planning/lane_driving/behavior_planning -p use_sim_time:=False -p wheel_radius:=0.3725 -p wheel_width:=0.215 -p wheel_base:=4.76012 -p wheel_tread:=1.754 -p front_overhang:=0.95099 -p rear_overhang:=1.52579 -p left_overhang:=0.26878 -p right_overhang:=0.26878 -p vehicle_height:=3.08 -p max_steer_angle:=0.64'].
pr_details: The function iterates over obstacle polygons, each containing segment indices (`bound_seg_idx`) that were calculated based on the **original** boundary's state before any modifications.
Inside the loop, `updated_bound.erase()` is called, which shrinks the size of the `updated_bound` vector.
In subsequent iterations, the pre-calculated indices from other obstacle polygons can become invalid (i.e., out of bounds) for the now-smaller `updated_bound` vector.
Calling `erase()` with iterators derived from these out-of-bounds indices results in undefined behavior, leading to the observed segmentation fault.
[Internal test scenario](https://evaluation.tier4.jp/evaluation/reports/9c923240-988c-57c7-be86-4c5df263f09b?project_id=x2_dev) passes 2248/2832, no degration

pr_title: fix(autoware_overlay_rviz_plugin): fix conflicting header file overlay_utils.hpp
pr_contents: The two packages `autoware_overlay_rviz_plugin` and `autoware_mission_details_overlay_rviz_plugin` conflicts on a header file of the same name `overlay_utils.hpp`. It's discovered when I attempted to create Debian packages for the two in this [work](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/autoware-debian-packaging). The `dpkg` package manager refuses to install both packages due to file conflict. To resolve this, this patch wraps headers files of respective packages inside a inner directory.

When compiling Autoware following the [source installation instructions](https://autowarefoundation.github.io/autoware-documentation/main/installation/autoware/source-installation/), add the option `--merge-install` to `colcon build` so that it merges compiled package directories. Check if `install/include` has two new directories `autoware_overlay_rviz_plugin` and `autoware_mission_details_overlay_rviz_plugin`.

pr_contents: This filter provides selective downsampling that preserves detailed point data in critical regions while reducing overall point cloud density:

The main purpose is to detect long-range stationary vehicles on the road, such as those stopped at an intersection or traffic light. With the point cloud densifier node, points at a distance will be densified and downsampling will not be applied in this densified area thanks to the roi excluded voxel-based downsampling operation.

pr_details_more: Points are classified based on their position relative to a defined Region of Interest (ROI)
Points inside the ROI are preserved at their original density (no downsampling)
Points outside the ROI undergo standard voxel grid downsampling
The final output combines both sets of points

pr_title: fix(route_handler): creating route at parking lot
pr_contents: At current autoware, the parking scenario cannot initiate sometimes due to route cannot be planned between ego lanelet and closest lanelet to goal pose. However since ego vehicle and goal pose in same parking lot area, we don't need to reject goal due to path planning.
This PR checks whether the start and goal poses are in the same parking lot and sends the start lanelet as the path to initiate other nodes, as a full path is not necessary for freespace planning.

[autoware_remaining_distance_time_calculator](https://github.com/autowarefoundation/autoware.universe/tree/main/planning/autoware_remaining_distance_time_calculator) package fails to calculate the time since the package cannot find a route between start and goal lanelet:
I am planning to create another PR to disable time calculation in the parking scenario, as the calculation no required during freespace driving.

Thank you for your PR. I am considering whether tensorrt_batched_nms should be a standalone package or add to the tensorrt_common. Any ideas?

I am not sure if it would be beneficial to use it as a separate package. When we organize it as a separate package, I would expect it to be used by multiple packages or models. Normally, the [batchedNMSPlugin](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT/tree/release/10.3/plugin/batchedNMSPlugin) is a plugin published within the TensorRT library, and the version we are using has been modified by **mmdeploy**. Therefore, I don't think it will be used by another model or package in the future. If this plugin is used, it will most likely be in its original form and I guess we can directly reach the original form from TensorRT headers.

Apart from that, if we want to gather all currently used and future plugins within `tensorrt_common`, this seems reasonable to me, but it is equally reasonable to keep it within the package. So, both of them OK for me (keep current form or put it to `tensorrt_common`).
Your reasoning is solid. I agree to keep it as its current form.

I discussed with the members of TIER IV and concluded that the formats of the metadata.yaml for PCD and Lanelet2 should be consistent.
So, please fit the format with [PCD's metadata.yaml](https://github.com/autowarefoundation/autoware.universe/tree/main/map/map_loader#metadata-structure).

Instead of using `origin_lat` and `origin_lon`, we will use `origin_x` and `origin_y`. Please convert the latitude and longitude to plane coordinates using the same coordinate system as the PCD file. In many cases, we use MGRS.
@StepTurtle Additionally, we would like `autoware_dynamic_lanelet_provider` to be separated from this PR.

Currently, `behavior_planner` receives the map topic from `autoware_dynamic_lanelet_provider`. However, please change it so that `behavior_planner` calls the `/map/get_differential_lanelet_map` service to receive the necessary map area.
This also aims to unify the architecture with the PCD map_loader side.

If there are any implementation or processing load issues, we would like to consider an interface that distributes submaps, similar to `autoware_dynamic_lanelet_provider`. Additionally, if that happens, we plan to consider submap distribution for PCD as well, in order to unify the architecture.
Step 1: Modify `behavior_planner` directly call the `/map/get_differential_lanelet_map` service and receive the map. `autoware_dynamic_lanelet_provider` to be separated from this PR.
Step 2: By implementing the planner to directly call the service, investigate if there are any issues such as increased complexity or processing load.

Step 3: If there are issues identified in the above step, consider implementing `autoware_dynamic_lanelet_provider` as part of the map module and adding the submap topic as the official map interface. If submap is to be the official interface, define and implement submap as the official interface for PCD as well.

For point cloud dynamic loading, the map loader service implemented in `ndt_scan_matcher` and only `ndt_scan_matcher` needs to dynamically loaded point cloud. So, I think if we remove `autoware_dynamic_lanelet_provider` from there and put into `behavior_planner`, we should run a node for `autoware_dynamic_lanelet_provider` on planning side. And I am not sure we want to run a separate node for this in planning.

Below is the diagram of the architecture we at TIER IV are considering.
As you are concerned, both the behavior_path_planner and behavior_velocity_planner will need the functionality to dynamically load the map, and the implementation will likely be almost identical.

- behavior_path_planner and behavior_velocity_planner require almost the same map, so there is no need to call the map separately
- The CPU processing load and memory consumption for the ROS Service are wasteful
I would like to share this with the TIER IV members and discuss it again.

Having a structure that distributes the map seemed meaningful for this reason, and I'm not sure how appropriate it would be to place this structure somewhere on the planning. Because of these reasons putting a package in map components was a good idea for us.
Also, Can I ask you to why TIER IV members wants to change current proposal.

Is the reason for your request to make it similar with  dynamic point cloud loading? or is it that we don't want a separate package for dynamic lanelet2 loading? If so, I wasn't in favor of having a separate package either, but doing these tasks on the planning side seems more incorrect to me.

pr_contents: Current support for backward trajectories is fairly limited and sometimes just happen to work "by accident" (e.g. some calculated data is wrong but mostly unused). In particular, I have found many backward driving issues with the `motion_velocity_smoother` node while implementing a new freespace planner.

Most functions in `motion_velocity_smoother` have been implemented with forward trajectories in mind and don't apply to backward trajectories. The "trick" currently used to handle backward trajectories is to "flip" the trajectory points velocity before processing it, to do as if the vehicle was driving forward and not backward, and then flip the output back. I think the idea is valid, however it is not properly implemented: for example [it causes steering values to be incorrect on backward trajectories](https://github.com/autowarefoundation/autoware.universe/issues/5976#issuecomment-1870862114).

The "proper" way to implement the flipping trick is not just to flip the velocity but to flip everything: trajectory pose orientation, velocity, steering... but also the ego pose and velocity when we need to place ego vehicle on the flipped trajectory.

Note that the way the logic is implemented at the moment (local trajectory but global `is_reverse_` parameter) is error prone and difficult to maintain. It would be worth packing trajectory data and ego state inside a single ("flippable") struct so that sub functions could just assume everything goes forward.
With the freespace planner in the planning simulator:
Except for these, there should be no other visible behavior change.

pr_comments: @NorahXiong If you could check the PR here it would be very helpful.
I think the PR did not totally resolve the problem as no dynamic-size costmap strategy is implemented.
Have the goal ever run out of the costmap during the test? (Not sure about that point, maybe a test video could be pasted.)
@NorahXiong The previous algorithm searches a path only included in the initial costmap but actually as the car moves, so does the cost map. Then the goal position sometimes goes out of the costmap.
This PR solves it so that the goal is never missed even if the map moves with the car.
I think we don't have to implement a dynamic-size cost map.

The [modification of the collision detection method ](https://github.com/TakumIto/autoware.universe/blob/fix/freespace_planner_out_of_range/planning/freespace_planning_algorithms/src/abstract_algorithm.cpp#L210-L244)is a little confusing to me. There might be small logical flaws cause it is more like a specific-bug-oriented patch. Actually, this PR did resolve the case in the original issue but I constructed another corner case as below:
1. Put an obstacle to force the trajectory planned.
2. The parking motion stuck in the last trajectory segment while the goal going out of costmap.
The initial and goal poses are pasted here in case you want to reproduce.

- `ros2 topic pub --once /planning/mission_planning/goal geometry_msgs/msg/PoseStamped "{header: {stamp: {sec: 0.0, nanosec: 0.0}, frame_id: map}, pose: {position: {x: 3751.814453125, y: 73737.5390625, z: 0.0}, orientation: {x: 0.0, y: 0.0, z: -0.9681636893299471, w: 0.25031793915543815}}}"`

In my environment(in the revised program), your new corner case doesn't occur and any varid path is not found.
Before this revising, we found an invalid path and the ego moved to a position where the goal was not unreachable.
After this PR, invalid paths are not found anyway. But in terms of preventing inappropriate paths before they happen, I think this is not degrading. How about your idea.

And In my opinion dynamical-size costmap is not appropriate. Because In practical situations, the perception area is limited by sensor limitations and obstacles. So in parking, the goal position should be in the recognizable area: fixed-size costmap according to egos performance.

pr_contents: As mentioned before internally, I think that the computations regarding the offsets produced by the `vibrations` are incorrect. The effect is small when the ROIs are near the optical center but increases as the ROIs get away from it.

pr_comments: Could you please provide slides or something to explain the computation?
I don't know how to read the figure, so please tell me. :pray:
Where is it on the image to be projected?
If the blue line is where the image is projected to, then why not leave it as it is now?

It is not "good" to represent the camera projection plane at an arbitrary such as in the blue line (unless it is the same distance for multiple examples) since it can be easy to arrive to misleading conclusions. Additionally, I think is better to understand this problem in the camera coordinate system rather than in the image space (forgetting the projection model for a while)
The current way to compute things it is not wrong per se, it is just not what it says it seeks to do.
A way to see the problem clearly is considering a very wide FOV and the  TLR in the border of the image. In that case:
- The z component is almost null compared with the x component which is very large (in camera coordinates)

- With the current way to compute things no matter how large we select the vibration yaw parameter the delta x does not really change. `delta_x = sin(vibration_yaw) * z`. Since `z << x`, no choice of `vibration_yaw` has an relative effect on `x`.
With the current cameras it is not really a problem, but as we move to higher resolutions (larger distances) and wider FOVs, the effect will be less easy to ignore.

It is always a choice to not adopt this way of computing the deltas since none of our products are really in need of it right now and adding this fix may cause concerns of man-hours (I don't think that is the case, but even so).

However, I would like at least for the people involved to be aware of the limitations of the current way we compute these deltas so that is we have issues in the future, we know what and how to address it.

pr_title: feat(route_handler) Rework path design to support when goal is behind start pose
pr_contents: <!-- Write a brief description of this PR. -->

The initial scope for this PR was to simply support the "goal is behind start pose on the same or neighbor lanelet" case. During my investigation, I realized this corner case is VERY difficult to implement and maintain if we keep the current way paths have been designed in Autoware planning modules.

In Autoware planning modules, a path is most of the time a `lanelet::ConstLanelets` (i.e. a list of lanelets). Because a list of lanelet is not adapted to describe paths (no start/goal point, not easy to manipulate, etc), if I where to keep the current design to fix the "goal is behind start" bug, I would basically need to add a lot of code in every single planning function, and most likely add a lot of bugs at the same time. It would also mean people maintaining or implementing planning functions would be required to think constantly about all possible corner cases (such as "goal is behind start") while working on the code. Such cognitive burden is not desirable.

Instead, I solve the "goal is behind start" issue (and hopefully many other planning bugs) by improving Autoware path design. The planning engineer will not have to do anything special: such corner case will be handled natively from now on. I introduce the following concepts:
I have implemented a simple, yet safe and efficient API (hopefully) to manipulate each of them. A few examples:

With this new API, it is no longer required to manipulate lanelets, points or even indices by yourself! Do you need to query a point within a path/route? Do you need to extend the path 10 meters backward? Do you need to make sure there is enough distance forward to do a lane change? Do you need to generate drivable area? You can do everything now with just a couple lines of code. The new classes will do the heavy lifting for you and make sure you don't accidently break something.

Each of these functions is meant to be safe, in the sense they either succeed and produce a valid path, or fail and return an empty object. As a consequence, it is not possible to create "broken" paths using the provided functions (for example, a path that would loop).

In some special cases, the functions will also try to "repair" broken paths. For instance, if you try to concatenate two overlapping paths with `concatenate`, the function will detect and try fix the overlap (because paths are not allowed to overlap themselves). If the concatenation or overlap fixing fails, an empty path will be returned. Such path fixing functionality is only required in the following cases:

In either case, an extra `overlap_removal_strategy` argument can be set to specify how overlaps should be fixed (keep everything at the beginning of the path, or at the end of the path, or split overlapped part and share it evenly, etc)
I have tried to reduce the API to the strict minimum. Still, I think the API provides all the bricks required to implement any complex planning function.

Much of the `LaneletRoute` code originates to `route_handler`. Because many functions within `behavior_path_planner` relies on the old `route_handler`, I also had to reimplement some of it with the new API. Migrating the old planning code to the new API is out of scope of the present PR (which is too big already), but there are many convoluted functions within `behavior_path_planner` modules which could be reduced in just a few (safe) lines, and I think it is definitely worth doing it in the future.
At the moment, the new types are all in `route_handler` package. There is no specific reason for that. The code could be moved to a better place in another PR.
All this for the route and path planner to support the "goal is begin pose" scenario natively.

pr_comments: If anyone is checking this PR, I still want to modify the design a bit.

In current PR state, it is "too" easy to get a list of lanelets from a `LaneletPath`, which should be avoided because a list of lanelets is not a good way to describe a path (that is the whole point of the PR). Instead, I want `LaneletPath` to be a `std::vector<LaneletSection>`, where `LaneletSection` is a type that describe a section within a lanelet (i.e. `{lanelet, start_arc_length, end_arc_length}`)

Although it requires slightly more changes to the `behavior_path_planner` code, I think it will make the code more robust. In particular, corner cases such as "the goal is behind start" would work without the need for the planning function engineer to think about it.

I think my path API has all the functionality the planning modules ever need. What is left is to use it so that corner cases such as "goal is behind start" is never a problem again. Unfortunately, there are maybe thousands LoC to change... I can't do it alone...
In particular, it is getting difficult to keep my work stable when other people are changing the planner modules at the same time.
Currently, there is a strange zigzag in near goal pose when a lane change is possible:
Except that, I think it is working good. So I guess @mitsudome-r you could already review it.
The description with images helps me a lot to understand the implementation.
Although we really appreciate your PR I have discussed with @TakaHoribe on this, and had several concerns:
* refactoring of the package takes quite a lot of time for us to review.

* We are also considering updating the behavior path planner on the background https://github.com/autowarefoundation/autoware/discussions/3097 which also makes us difficult to merge this at the moment.
Also, we were thinking of different approach to solve the issue by modifying mainly mission_planner rather than adding new Lanelet classes.
* Whenever mission_planner detects a loop in a path, it will only send route to behavior planners until the lane just before the loop.
* As vehicle drives along the route and no longer have a loop, it will update the route until the goal.

Although we have to check if the behavior planner can handle update of route while driving, it would make implementation much simpler. Also, we can also handle route with multiple loops, not only the route with goal point behind starting point.
What do you think about the approach?
Hi, I totally get it. I know to change the API may be tricky and cumbersome (and add many bugs).
I never thought about sending partial routes. It could be a thing, although changing the route while the vehicle is driving also comes with its own problems. I could poke this after the holidays.

Although I first started to work on this PR to fix the "goal behind start pose" issue, the proposed changes go way beyond that "simple" case. In particular, it is also a way to write `behavior_path_planner` functions in a simpler and (hopefully) safer way. The more I worked on the planning functions, the more I am convinced the modules would benefit from a better abstraction than just a list of lanelets.
Take it as a message in a bottle. The proposed classes could improve the `route_handler`, or some parts salvaged and reused for new planning functions, or just ignored and thrown in the bin 😅
So if I understand your idea, this is how it could be implemented:

* Add support for "goal behind start" use case (like in https://github.com/autowarefoundation/autoware.universe/pull/2425 or https://github.com/autowarefoundation/autoware.universe/issues/1715#issuecomment-1318155064). This route may contains loops (e.g. `1->2->3->4->1`).
* Move the route publishing logic to a new timer callback function (from `MissionPlanner::change_route`). The new function will:
* Check the position of the vehicle on the route
* Remove from the route all sections before current lanelet.
* If the route has been modified, publish the route up to the first duplicated lanelet (e.g. `1->2->3->4`).
* after the ego vehicle has reached `2`, timer callback send `2->3->4->1`
* after the ego vehicle has reached `3`, the timer callback send `3->4->1`
* after the ego vehicle has reached `1` again, the timer callback send `1`
Although it should work, I have several concerns regarding this method:
* At the end of the day, it is a hacky solution to cope with `motion_planner` not supporting looped lanelet ids.

* This assumes the global route can be changed freely while driving. For example, if the ego vehicle is on lanelet `2`, does the planner generates exactly the same path when the route is `1->2->3` and `2->3`? Other modules may also react on a route change (e.g. new route = new mission).

* Currently, Autoware requires a (remote) operator to validate the route and engage the vehicle. But with this change, the full route is not known anymore (even though its just 1 lanelet missing here). In other words, Autoware could then change the route without any human validation.

* The "Check the position of the vehicle on the route" is actually tricky to implement correctly. For instance, on which route lanelet is the vehicle when several lanelets overlap within the route? For example in the situation below, the ego vehicle is slightly out of the route (e.g. because the operator moved the vehicle manually or autoware moved the vehicle off-road to avoid an obstacle), and lanelet `1` and `2` within the path are overlapped:

What if the `(out of path)` is a `3`, and the route is something like `1->2->3`? The ego vehicle is initially on `1`, but while avoiding an obstacle, it gets close to `3` and may think it is on `3`, thus skipping the `1->2` route entirely. There are countless corner cases like this.
For most lanelet maps, there should not be any problem. But if there is, Autoware will just break. What do you think?
Currently, TIER IV is trying to support goal modification at run time due to other needs so I believe we will make the change to the other modules as needed.

At least, mission_planner should be aware of the whole route anyways so it can still publish visualization marker of the full route regardless of the route. It can also publish global route as a different topic if it is needed for debug purpose.

I believe this issue already exists with the current implementation anyways regardless of the looped route issue(There could be overlapping lanes at intersections). Therefore, I think we should be handling this as a separate issue.
Thank you for the details. Should I wait for the goal modification at runtime feature to be available or should I have a head start on this?
@TakaHoribe Do we have any timeline about when we support mission_planner goal modification at runtime?
We will wait for goal modification implementation to finish, discussed in [Proposal for handling goal modification](https://github.com/autowarefoundation/autoware/discussions/2983)
It is in the final stage for the implementation. Then this PR will be reworked, hopefully it will be much simpler after the discussion above is resolved.

pr_details: Refactor route_handler package: add new class LaneletPoint, LaneletSection, LaneletPath, LaneletRoute. All these new class act as safe wrapper over path related concepts.
With the new API, planning functions should no longer need to manipulate lanelets, indices, points, etc directly.
`LaneletSection`: a section of a lanelet centerline. Basically: `{lanelet, start_arc_length, end_arc_length}`

`LaneletPath`: a safe wrapper for `std::vector<LaneletSection>`. There are many constraints on `LaneletPath` (consistent with current Autoware path design). For example, except the first and last section, all inner section must cover the whole lanelet. For example, all section must be connected, either directly (next section lanelet follows the previous section one), or indirectly (next section alnelet follows a neighbor of the previous section). Loops and overlaps are not allowed (but first and last sections may be on the same lanelet).

`LaneletRoute`: a safe wrapper over route building and query functions. A route is essentially and list of reachable lanelets and a main/preferred path. Many of these functions existed already in `route_handler` and have just be moved/improved in `LaneletRoute`.

`LaneletRoute` has `getStraightPath(lanelet_point, forward_distance, backward_distance)` function to query "straight" path within the route (i.e. no lane change), and `extendPath(path, forward_distance, backward_distance)` function to safely extend a path forward/backward. Optional `within_route=false` arguments can be used to query path beyond the route boundaries (typically use to extend path before/after start/goal point.)
`LaneletRoute` has `getRemainingForwardLengthWithinRoute(lanelet_point)` to measure the forward distance left before we leave the route (either reached dead end or reached the goal).
when optional argument `within_route` is set to `false`. For example in `getStraightPath` and `extendPath`.

pr_title: Add Differential Drive Motor Package for Enhanced DeepRacer Control
pr_contents: This PR introduces a comprehensive differential drive motor package (`aws-deepracer-community-diffdrive-motor-pkg`) that replaces the traditional servo-based steering system with a two-motor differential drive approach. This enhancement provides more precise control and opens up new possibilities for advanced robotic applications.
This package is designed as a drop-in replacement:
**Related Issues**: This addresses the need for improved motor control in custom DeepRacer builds and provides better hardware platform support for the community.
pr_details: **DifferentialDriveController**: Converts servo commands to motor speeds using differential drive kinematics
**Turning Logic**: Outer wheel maintains commanded speed, inner wheel speed is reduced based on turning radius
pr_details_more: Converts servo-style commands (angle + throttle) to left/right motor speeds
Implements proper differential drive kinematics for realistic vehicle behavior
Configurable turning radius constraints and motor response curves
**Raspberry Pi**: Full support for Waveshare Motor Driver HAT with TB6612FNG H-bridge
**Original DeepRacer**: Compatible with existing DeepRacer hardware via PWM channels
Platform auto-detection and configuration
Maintains identical ROS2 interfaces as the original servo package
Drop-in replacement requiring no changes to existing applications
Preserves calibration workflows and service APIs
**MotorManager**: Hardware abstraction for TB6612FNG motor driver control

pr_title: Version 2.1.9 - Ubuntu 24.04 on original AWS DeepRacer & more
pr_contents: This release introduces several important improvements and new features for the AWS DeepRacer Community Custom Car stack.

This release significantly improves system reliability, adds essential time management capabilities, and enhances camera functionality. The power management changes ensure DeepRacer systems remain consistently available, while the new time API enables better system administration and logging. The new security features allow for encrypted, secure-boot capable DeepRacer images. Most importantly, this release brings Ubuntu 24.04 and OpenVINO support to the original AWS DeepRacer hardware, unlocking better performance and modern software compatibility.
pr_details: **Ubuntu 24.04 (Noble) Support**: Added full support for Ubuntu 24.04 on the original AWS DeepRacer hardware (Intel Atom).
**Intel OpenVINO Integration**: Implemented a new inference backend using modern OpenVINO as legacy interface is no longer available.
**New Image Creation Script**: Added `create-image.sh` for automated disk image generation (loopback or physical).
**TPM2 Integration**: Secure boot support with TPM2 key unsealing (`tpm2-initramfs-hook`, `tpm2-unseal-keyscript`).
**Flashing Utilities**: New tools (`usb_flash.sh`, `seal_and_luksChangeKey.sh`) for flashing and sealing keys.
**Integrated Logging Solution**: Replaced external `larsll-deepracer-logging` dependency with a new internal community-maintained package.
**C++**: High-performance native implementation optimized for ROS2 Jazzy (80-90% less CPU usage, 40-60% lower memory footprint).
**Features**: Automatic recording, USB storage detection, configurable modes (`Never`, `USBOnly`, `Always`), and dynamic bag file naming.
pr_details_more: **Platform Enhancements**:
Optimized TensorFlow build for x86 Atom processors.
Improved device detection and platform identification.
Enhanced hardware control scripts (PWM, LED, OTG).
**Encryption Support**: Added optional LUKS encryption for the ROOT partition.
**Dual Implementation**:
**Python**: Fully compatible with ROS2 Humble and earlier.
**NEW**: Added comprehensive time and timezone management functionality
`/api/get_time` - Get current time and timezone information
`/api/set_timezone` - Set system timezone
Full timezone validation and error handling
Support for timezone abbreviations and UTC offsets
**IMX708 Camera Enhancement**: Added auto-focus support for IMX708 cameras
Enabled `AfMode = 2` and `AfPause = 2` parameters
Improved image quality for newer Raspberry Pi camera modules
**Code Cleanup**: Removed unused imports and simplified camera service remappings
**Power Management**: Disabled sleep, suspend, hibernate, and hybrid-sleep targets on Raspberry Pi
Prevents unexpected system sleep during racing sessions
Ensures consistent system availability
**Webserver Robustness**: Enhanced error handling for webserver node initialization
Added null checks and exception handling for webserver_node references
Prevents crashes when webserver node is not yet initialized
Better graceful degradation during startup
**Flask Dependencies**: Added Flask web framework dependencies to dev containers
`flask`, `flask-cors`, `flask-wtf` packages added
Supports Ubuntu 22.04 (Humble) and 24.04 (Noble) environments

Better file exclusion patterns for build artifacts
Cleaner development experience

Better handling of distribution-specific package names
More robust version string construction

pr_contents: This PR adds the `standard-imghdr` dependency to `requirements.txt` to make build compatible in newer (>3.13) Python environments while at the same time abiding to the `sphinx==5.0`.

When building the Sphinx documentation with the [sphinxdoc/sphinx](https://hub.docker.com/r/sphinxdoc/sphinx) Docker  image (same happens when using the latest [Python image](https://hub.docker.com/_/python)) I noticed errors stating that a Python module was missing:
This error does not appear in CI because the Github build pipeline uses an older version of Python:

The module `imghdr` has been deprecated in Python 3.11 and completely removed in Python 3.13 (see [Removed Modules](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/removed.html) and [PEP 0594](https://peps.python.org/pep-0594/#deprecated-modules).
Navigate to the `docs` directory and start the Python (or Sphinx) Docker container (for Sphinx replace `python:3` with `sphinxdoc/sphinx`):
Then, inside the Docker, install the dependencies:
Finally, try building the documentation with (you're already in the `docs` directory):
The result should be the following error
Try rebuilding now and the error is gone.

To test backwards compatibility, checkout this branch that adds `standard-imghdr` to the `requirements.txt` file. Then, repeat the process described above with an older version of Python. For instance, use the image for Python 3.8:

This error arises mainly due to defining relatively old versions of both Sphinx (`==5.0`) and Python (`==3.8`). I also tested building the documentation with a newer version of Sphinx and did not notice any build errors. However, I think that adding `standard-imghdr` to the `requirements.txt` is a smaller change and less likely to disrupt anything.

pr_contents: We wanted to try a setup where the bitbots_main repo is the colcon workspace itself. This would make a few workspace related settings easier, fix the vscode ROS extention, clean up the repo top level and allow us to have all commands at the same level (managed now via `just` instead of make, as it e.g. supports positional args).
pr_comments: I agree that having the `build` and `install` folders  can lead to a bit of clutter, but when navigating the workspace during use the folder structure is nearly identical to a normal workspace setup and due to these folders being git ignored, the upstream repo is tidy, maybe even more so since all code now lives in a source folder, which would otherwise result in an additional nesting.

Also afaik many build systems like e.g. cargo store their artifacts inside an ignored folder of the repo by default, so it should be familiar for many people. The code lives in the source folder which can still be searched. The folder structure stays the same. Essentially only the `.git` folder moves upwards.

We already do this using the lib folder inside the repo. All third party packages are already placed there. And for non Bit-Bots related things, like e.g. a fix for ros2 itself I always create a second workspace to isolate things. There are also many cases where having the colcon workspace as a repo is a bad idea imo.. E.g. at tams there are many repos for the different robots, sensors etc. and if you do an experiment you clone them inside your colcon workspace. But with the mono repo I think it is okay to couple the Bit-Bots workspace together with our code.

What would be benefits of symlinked code? I know some people do this, but I do not see that many practical advantages. I would argue that it is a good thing that the directory structure is standardized by the repo, this way the scrips etc can expect a certain configuration without relying too much on global often not directly version controlled configuration.  My ideal setup would be one where you clone the repo, build it and everything works, creating minimal friction.

I have often seen especially new people struggle with where which command should run (make commands vs. colcon). Aliases helped a bit there, but they also implicitly change directories etc.. My intention was to unify this by having one top-level repo where everything can be performed.

Also what started this idea was that the vscode ros extension now requires that the whole workspace is open in vs code, which requires that the preconfigured settings live in the colon ws, which is unlucky as we have them inside the repo. Yeah we could symlink, but that also increases the complexity. Having the settings at the workspace level also allows for a few other nice configs.
Also this reduces additional setup like creating a workspace with the correct folder structure upon setup etc.. This is mostly automated right now, but it would be neat if we wouldn't need that.

Non Ros/package related scripts can live in their own scripts directory that is not part of the colon environment that way reducing potential friction points, as we had issues in the past where colcon tried to build e.g. an unrelated setup.py.

This configuration also allows us to have a command runner that executes all relevant commands for typical usage cases from one place. This removes issues where colcon is called from the wrong directory, people don't know what commands exist, it brings the documentation of the common commands close to the code so they are less likely outdated and it allows for shorter commands. Parts of this can also be achieved using a alias, but this seems like a better solution. Many projects have a make file to setup, clean, ....

The main idea was to reduce friction along the most taken usage paths, especially for beginners. Removing the notation of an explicit workspace might help there and allow for less moving parts overall. But I am also a bit cautious of a migration like this, as it might break existing bashrc configurations etc..
Wow, thanks for the detailed explanation.

I'm not against the change, just wanted to understand your intentions. I agree, that it is probably easier for new members to not have to worry about the difference of `make`/`just` and actual `colcon` commands at first.
Seeing as the Vscode ROS extension requires the workspace, I think this makes a lot of sense.
I think you misunderstood what I meant. I was just talking about the current status quo where e.g. `~/colcon_ws/src/bitbots_main -> ~/git/bitbots/bitbots_main`.
This just ensures, that you have a single expectable `$COLCON_WS` and no matter what project you just symlink to `target` in `~/colcon_ws/src/target`.
But yeah I agree as we just use the monorepo normally this change makes a lot of sense :+1:
Okay, what' left to do? We have to rebase this and adapt some docs and tools, right? Then, when merging, write some instructions on how to work with the new setup.

Yeah maybe update some docs / test them. I already adjusted most of the docs. There are some open items regarding default location of the repo and how we deal with the COLCON_WS env variable. We could also consider using direnv and move some of the zshrc stuff there. Also the robot_compile stript will be broken and we might want to test it on e.g. amy.

The newly introduced script `urdf_to_mujoco.py` is designed to convert a URDF (Unified Robot Description Format) file into a MuJoCo (Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact) XML model file. The script begins by defining the input URDF file path and the actuator types along with their mappings and default settings. It checks for the existence of the specified URDF file and parses it using the `lxml` library.

A `mujoco` tag is added to the URDF to ensure compatibility with MuJoCo, followed by rendering the URDF as a string and loading it into a MuJoCo model. The model is then saved as a temporary XML file, which is subsequently parsed into an `etree` structure for further modifications.

Key modifications include restructuring the world body by creating a new body named "torso" and transferring all existing elements into it, along with adding a free joint and a light source. The script also assigns classes to geometries based on their attributes, differentiating between visual and collision classes. Default settings for sites, geometries, actuators, and joints are defined and added to the XML structure.

The script removes certain attributes from joints, such as damping and friction loss, and assigns a class based on the actuator mapping. Actuators are then added to the top level of the XML structure. Finally, the modified XML is saved to a file with a `.xml` extension, corresponding to the original URDF file name.
Overall, the script encapsulates the entire process of converting a URDF file into a MuJoCo-compatible XML format, including necessary adjustments and enhancements to the model structure.

It includes a comprehensive structure detailing the robot's components, including joints, bodies, and geometries. The model specifies default properties for various joint types, such as damping, armature, and friction loss, for different actuators (e.g., `mx106`, `mx64`, `xh-540`).

The asset section lists numerous mesh files that represent the physical components of the robot, such as the torso, arms, legs, and various connectors. The world body section outlines the hierarchical structure of the robot, detailing the position and orientation of each body part, including the torso, shoulders, arms, hips, legs, and neck. Each body is defined with its inertial properties, joints, and geometries, which include visual and collision representations.

The actuator section specifies the control interfaces for the robot's joints, indicating which joints can be controlled and their corresponding actuator classes. The model also includes a light source targeting the torso, enhancing the simulation environment.
Overall, this file encapsulates the complete definition of the robotic model, including its physical structure, joint configurations, and control mechanisms.

The new file `mujoco_env.py` introduces the `WolfgangMujocoEnv` class, which defines an OpenAI Gym environment for simulating the Wolfgang robot using the MuJoCo physics engine. The class initializes by loading a robot model from an XML file and setting up the simulation data and rendering capabilities. It extracts joint and actuator names from the model, defines action and observation spaces, and establishes a unique environment name.

The `reset` method resets the simulation state and returns the initial observation. The `_get_obs` method retrieves the current joint positions for observations. The `step` method applies actions to the robot, updates the simulation for a specified number of steps, and calculates a reward based on the robot's position. It also handles rendering the simulation frame using OpenCV.
The `render` method updates and displays the simulation frame based on the specified render mode. The `close` method cleans up resources by deleting the model, data, and renderer objects.
The main execution block creates an instance of the environment, resets it, and runs a loop for 1000 steps, sampling random actions and displaying the rendered frames.

The new file `sb3_mujoco.py` introduces functionality for training and evaluating a reinforcement learning model using the Stable Baselines3 library with a Mujoco environment. It begins by importing the necessary modules, including `WolfgangMujocoEnv` from `mujoco_env`, and sets up a vectorized environment using `make_vec_env` with one environment instance. A Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) model is instantiated with a multi-layer perceptron policy (`MlpPolicy`) and configured to use 512 steps per update. The model is trained for 20,000 steps with logging enabled at every step.

After training, the environment is reset, and a loop runs for 1,000 iterations where the model predicts actions based on the current observations. The environment steps through the predicted actions, collecting rewards and checking for termination conditions. If the episode ends, the environment is reset. Additionally, every 10 iterations, the environment is rendered visually for human observation. Finally, the environment is closed after the loop completes.

pr_quotes: Please add one entry in this file for each change in Yarn's behavior. Use the same format for all entries, including the third-person verb. Make sure you don't add more than one line of text to keep it clean. Thanks!
- Passes arguments following `--` when running a workspace script (`yarn workspace pkg run command -- arg`)
- Prints workspace names with `yarn workspaces` (silence with `-s`)
- Implements `yarn set version <version>` as an alias for `policies set-version`
- Fixes an issue where the archive paths were incorrectly sanitized
- Allows some dots in binary names again
- Better error handling on `yarn set version`
- Folders like `.cache` won't be pruned from the `node_modules` after each install.
- Correctly installs workspace child dependencies when workspace child not symlinked to root.
- Makes running scripts with Plug'n Play possible on node 13.

Implementation of `MrsLib_ErrorGraph`  and `MrsLib_ErrorPublisher` : public interfaces added into `mrs_lib` to provide a centralized error monitoring and root cause analysis.
Providing routines for nodes to report errors (error_publisher) and a centralized node (Errorgraph) to aggregate into a the errors into dependency graph and identify root errors.
The node will publish the error message in its own topic (typically ~errors). These messages can be taken by the centralized monitoring node node or subscribing directly.
The ErrorPublisher class provides four methods for reporting different categories of errors.
Method | Primary Use Case | Deduplication Strategy | Error Type Generated
addGeneralError | Custom application-specific errors with unique IDs | ID-based replacement | Custom string (description)
addOneshotError | Initialization errors or unique failures | None (always added) | Custom string (description)
addWaitingForTopicError | Blocked waiting for ROS topic data | Topic name-based replacement | TYPE_WAITING_FOR_TOPIC
addWaitingForNodeError | Blocked waiting for another node's operation | Node ID-based replacement | TYPE_WAITING_FOR_NODE

**Centralized Aggregation**: The **`Diagnostics_Manager (TBD) `** node subscribes to all error topics
**Graph Construction**: The **`Errorgraph`** class builds a dependency graph via **`add_element_from_msg()`**
pr_details_more: **Error Detection**: MRS components detect issues (missing topics, unresponsive nodes, timeouts)
**Local Aggregation**: Each component's **`ErrorPublisher`** instance batches errors locally
**Root Cause Analysis**:  DFS to identify error roots
**Filtered Output**: Only root causes are published as **`ErrorgraphElementArray`**

pr_contents: Currently webots_ros2 only builds natively on Ubuntu. Using Robostack, a partially supported ROS2 installation can also be done fairly easily directly on MacOS.
This pull requests makes some changes to the build process, so webots_ros2 also builds natively on MacOS.
This pull-request is pretty much WIP and not ready to be merged yet.
Note that for testing purposes I made changes to the reduced webots source code (the one generated by sync_controller_lib.sh) directly here in the repository.

Currently the build process for MacOS always targets an Application Bundle build, i.e., resources and dynamic libraries are expected to be prefixed with `Contents/...`. As webots_ros2_driver only targets linux for now, it however expects files to be in the unprefixed location. For now I solved this by only conditionally prefixing paths determined by the variable `BUILD_MACOS_BUNDLE`. This however requires changes in the build process of webots. Another solution would be to leave the paths as they are, and change only webots_ros2_driver to use the files under the Contents prefix.

Further note that I bumped the minimum cmake version to version 3.15 to fix a problem with findPython module during the build process. If this is undesirable I can look If I find a workaround that does not depend on a version bump.

@lalten looks fine. The MinGW CI failure is a flaky test, which we can ignore, but the Ubuntu bazel target fails.
I assigned @elBoberido since he may has some more insights here.
@lalten the bzlmod code came from a community member and I'm not that familiar with the code. Can you specify which  public targets are affected by the dev dependencies?
Buildifier is unconditionally depended on in the root BUILD
Googletest is depended on in a regular cc_library with public visibility:

Okay, the `buildifier` is definitely a dev dependency. The `iceoryx_hoofs_testing` is actually also a dev dependency but I'm not sure how this could be modeled with bazel. It is basically meant to be used for tests which use iceoryx. For example it contains a logger which suppresses all the output but if a test fails, it prints all log messages to help debugging.
Is there another way to mark this library as a dev dependency but still make it available to users?
In the end, I guess it should not matter and as long as one does depend only on e.g. `iceoryx_hoofs` bazel will not require `gTest` to be available. Please correct me if I'm wrong.

dev dependencies can not be depended on outside the root module, i.e. as soon as iceoryx is used as Bzlmod dependency of another project (which of course is the intended use case), dev dependencies are not there anymore.
<s>Note that Bazel will want to analyze the entire graph, so even if a user doesn't want to depend on iceoryx_hoofs_testing (or buildifier), these Bazel repos must be visible to the root module.</s>
Looks like the buildifier usage is actually ok, here is another repo with the same setup:

ERROR: Skipping '@org_eclipse_iceoryx//:iceoryx_binding_c': error loading package '@@org_eclipse_iceoryx~//': Unable to find package for @@[unknown repo 'buildifier_prebuilt' requested from @@org_eclipse_iceoryx~]//:rules.bzl: The repository '@@[unknown repo 'buildifier_prebuilt' requested from @@org_eclipse_iceoryx~]' could not be resolved: No repository visible as '@buildifier_prebuilt' from repository '@@org_eclipse_iceoryx~'.

ERROR: error loading package '@@org_eclipse_iceoryx~//': Unable to find package for @@[unknown repo 'buildifier_prebuilt' requested from @@org_eclipse_iceoryx~]//:rules.bzl: The repository '@@[unknown repo 'buildifier_prebuilt' requested from @@org_eclipse_iceoryx~]' could not be resolved: No repository visible as '@buildifier_prebuilt' from repository '@@org_eclipse_iceoryx~'.
ERROR: Build did NOT complete successfully
Okay, this is weird. Why should the `buildifier` be needed in order to build `iceoryx_hoofs`? Bazel has some weird dependency handling.
Do you have time to check it there is an obvious flaw in the bzlmod setup?
This is still required, without this patch consumers can not depend on the repo as a library.
The reason that buildifier_prebuilt must be available is that it is `load()`ed in https://github.com/eclipse-iceoryx/iceoryx/blob/7592b2adbf425d04a06d24571711e1a19a977d92/BUILD.bazel#L18

this BUILD must go through build graph analysis by all consumers of iceoryx as a library. Since iceoryx does not state a dependency on buildifier_prebuilt (dev_dependencies are invisible when not the root repo) this load fails and breaks the consumer's build graph.

I rebased the commit. There isn't really any drawback to just depending on buildifier and googletest. Users don't need to install anything or do any other action, Bazel will handle everything for them.
The change is completely transparent for developers of the repo who use it as root module, and it enables use of the repo as a library for downstream consumers.

Okay, just out of interest. Assuming I would not want to declare this as public dependency but keep it as dev dependency. Would it be possible to adjust the root `BUILD.bazel` file in a way to achieve this goal?
I think it may work if you only load() the buildifier repo in BUILD files that don't contain any targets that are dependencies of publicly visible targets. Would need to try that out.
Keep in mind consumers may actually want to run the tests (like in the presubmit CI of the BCR), so the BUILDs that contain the tests should work.

One approach is to have a separate MODULE.bazel for that that loads the main module from .. and adds googletest and friends as bazel_dep (example: https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel-central-registry/blob/019b40da8e5beb3071058bc57d76d0547c2258d9/modules/pcl/1.14.1/overlay/test/MODULE.bazel) but that is not great for developers wanting to work in the repo itself
Having the tests for the users is perfectly fine. It's the `buildifier` that is totally irrelevant to the consumers to the library.
Currently, the `bazel/BUILD.bazel` file is empty. Would it make sense to move the `buildifier` stuff to that file and keep it as dev_dependency?
tbh I don't think you need the buildifier to be part of the Bazel build graph at all. It's much more common to put it in pre-commit instead: https://github.com/warchant/pre-commit-buildifier

Agreed with the buildifier not being part of the bazel grahp. But since not all of our contributors are using bazel, we cannot rely on the commit hooks. A CI check would be sufficient, though. Could you add a buildifier action to the bazel job and adjust the `doc/website/advanced/installation-guide-for-contributors.md` file accordingly. Maybe add that one can get a prebuild version from `https://github.com/keith/buildifier-prebuilt/`. Then the buildifier could be removed from the bazel graph and `tools/ci/build-test-ubuntu-bazel.sh`.
If it is easier, it would also be fine to add the prebuild buildifier to `tools/ci/build-test-ubuntu-bazel.sh` instead of the github action.

pr_contents: PR should (at some point) enable to log any type of raw message and store it as an binary file. With this feature the driver would be able record the messages required for PPK as binaries.

pr_comments: We could definitely go that route. Then we can use the [sbp2rinex](https://support.swiftnav.com/support/solutions/articles/44001907895-sbp-to-rinex-converter-and-data-post-processing) pipeline.
A different approach could be to record the necessary ROS topics in a ros bag
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11293852/84487174-addd6780-ac9e-11ea-93ab-9931506731cd.png) and write a python programm to convert to rinex and call swiss topo corrections.

Thanks for reporting this issue and providing a detailed description!

At the image center, these values are identical, but they diverge toward the edges -- like a parabola.
